inputs.source: Engineering design docs (confidential; write restricted to engineers)
Jira tickets filed by customers, via planned MCP server integration

instructions.note: Secret/credential leakage is prevented only by a prompt instruction ('Never paste secrets or credentials into answers'), with no structural redaction or DLP control. Acceptable today given no egress channel exists, but this reliance should not be carried forward once web.fetch or other egress tools are added.

elements.name: Customer ticket content entering agent context (planned)

controls.name: No network egress exists in the current deployment
docs.search credential is read-only, least privilege
Replies are bound to the authenticated requester's own session
Chat client does not render images or fetch links in agent output
Write access to design docs restricted to engineers
Prompt rule: never paste secrets or credentials into answers
controls.decay_rationale: Relies entirely on the model choosing to omit secret-like content it reads from design docs; a more capable or adversarially prompted model can be argued into including it, especially once new egress exists.

controls.name: SSO authentication on inbound chat channel
Role or need-to-know check before disclosing confidential doc content
Network egress allowlist restricting web.fetch to vetted public documentation domains
Treat Jira ticket content as untrusted; block it from selecting tool arguments or triggering docs_search/web_fetch without confirmation
controls.decay_rationale: Isolation depends on classifying and filtering free-text ticket content; multi-turn or multi-document payloads and paraphrased instructions can get past content-based filtering even when enforced outside the model.

controls.name: Tamper-evident log correlating each tool call with the triggering input and requester identity

findings.title: Confidential design docs answered to any SSO-authenticated employee with no role or need-to-know check (T→S1)

forecast.watch_signal: docs.search scope expands to cover additional, more sensitive repositories, or the chat bot is opened beyond the current authenticated-employee audience.

evidence.observation: The prompt instructs the agent to answer engineering questions using docs.search for any request, with no role or need-to-know check on the requester.
Design docs are confidential with write access restricted to engineers, but no equivalent read restriction is described for who may query them through the bot.
Replies go only to the authenticated requester, bounding the audience to the asking employee, but that employee's entitlement to engineering design docs is not verified.

recommendations.action: Add a role or need-to-know check (e.g., engineering team membership) before including confidential design doc excerpts in a reply, independent of SSO authentication alone.

findings.title: No attributable record of which documents were disclosed to which employee

forecast.watch_signal: web.fetch or a Jira MCP server entry appears in the tool manifest/config without an accompanying tamper-evident audit log control.

evidence.observation: The system prompt describes answering and citation behavior but states no logging, audit, or provenance requirement for agent actions.
No audit record of which documents were read and disclosed to which employee is described in the runtime notes.

recommendations.action: Add a tamper-evident log recording each docs.search and chat reply with requester identity and timestamp, enforced outside the model.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1) if planned web.fetch and Jira MCP (customer tickets) are added: customer-authored ticket content could direct exfiltration of confidential design docs via web.fetch

attack_path.note: Customer-authored Jira ticket content enters the agent's context via the planned MCP server.
Agent reads confidential design docs while answering, potentially influenced by injected ticket instructions.
Planned tool can request an attacker-influenced URL carrying doc content in the query string, with no current allowlist or isolation control.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: web.fetch appears in the tool manifest, or a Jira MCP server entry (with customer-ticket read scope) appears in MCP client config.

evidence.observation: Roadmap text: 'add a web.fetch tool so answers can include public references, and connect a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers.' Customer-filed ticket text is untrusted content that would enter the agent's context, and web.fetch would give the agent its first egress channel.

'There is no network egress today' confirms the control that currently prevents any exfiltration path; adding web.fetch removes exactly this control, and no replacement destination allowlist or input-isolation control is described.

recommendations.action: Do not add web.fetch without a destination allowlist excluding user-writable/attacker-reachable URLs, and never construct the fetch URL from untrusted content such as Jira ticket text.

Before connecting the Jira MCP server, treat all ticket content (especially customer-filed tickets) as untrusted; keep it out of any path that can select tool arguments or trigger docs_search/web_fetch without additional confirmation.
Add a tamper-evident log correlating each tool call (docs_search, web_fetch) with the triggering input and requester identity, maintained outside model control.

stride_coverage.rationale: The chat client's method of authenticating the agent's own identity to employees is not described in the artifacts.
The agent cannot modify its own configuration (can_modify_own_config: false), and tool definitions are not described as externally mutable in this design.
No rate limit or step cap is described for docs.search, and the artifacts do not state whether the chat client throttles per-user requests.
The agent holds a single least-privilege read-only credential with no path to broader access; it cannot escalate its own permissions in this design.
No information is given about rate limits or quotas on reads of the design docs store.
The auth method for the planned Jira MCP server is not specified in the roadmap note (auth_method: unknown).
No logging or attribution approach for the planned Jira integration is described in the roadmap note.
No rate limit or step cap for the planned Jira integration is described in the roadmap note.
The planned integration does not grant the Jira server or ticket content any elevated credential; the agent's existing least-privilege read scope is reused, not escalated.
This flow carries content into the agent; the disclosure risk is on the outbound web.fetch flow (el.web_fetch_flow), not on this inbound ticket flow.
No information on rate limiting or volume controls for the planned Jira MCP integration is given.
Transport security (TLS, destination validation) for the planned web.fetch tool is not described in the roadmap note.
No rate limit or destination allowlist is specified yet for the planned outbound fetch capability.
Whether the planned Jira integration verifies customer identity on ticket submission is not described in the artifacts.
Attribution of ticket authorship for audit purposes is not described in the roadmap note.
The public internet destination is not a single identifiable peer whose spoofing is meaningful; the risk is an uncontrolled egress destination, captured in finding F3.
External public destinations are outside the organization's attribution boundary; the relevant concern is data exposure, captured in finding F3, not repudiation.

rating.rationale: Today the design keeps risk low: the only source reaching docs.search is the requester's own authenticated question (a trusted source), the docs.search credential is read-only, replies are bound to the authenticated requester with no link or image rendering, and critically there is no network egress at all, so no path can move confidential data outside the organization. The roadmap, however, describes adding a web.fetch tool (the agent's first egress channel) and a Jira MCP server that introduces customer-filed ticket content as a new untrusted input, with no destination allowlist, input isolation, or audit logging described for either. If both are built as described, the single control holding the line today -- the absence of any network egress -- is exactly what the new_tool trigger removes, reopening a lethal-trifecta path (untrusted ticket content → confidential doc read → arbitrary web egress) rated critical. A secondary, independent gap is the absence of any attributable record of which documents were disclosed to whom, which is low-consequence today (read-only, internal recipient) but would become high-consequence once an egress-capable tool exists.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in prompt.md and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; no logs, traces, or live configuration were reviewed.
No MCP/tool manifest or IaC was provided for the current deployment; capability scope (docs.search, chat reply) is inferred from the runtime notes and prompt text, so confidence is medium.

The planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are described only in a one-line roadmap note; their exact scope, authentication, and any planned mitigations are unknown, so the forecast finding (F3) uses worst-case assumptions consistent with rubric guidance for additive triggers.

No runtime or orchestration config was provided; the autonomy level (A3) and absence of approval gates are taken as implied by the design description, not verified against an actual execution harness.
